paragraphs.source_en: “Ha ha! ‘Have some tea’ is a little too severe. He must have thought that would be enough to put you properly in your place and leave you speechless. A splendid performance. We really ought to cry, Long live Lord Tendo Kohei!” The more Mr. Meitei spoke, the more amusing he found it, and he burst into hearty laughter. When the master learned that the sender of the letter he had read over and over with no small reverence was in fact a certified madman, he felt that all his earlier earnestness and painstaking effort had somehow been wasted, and this made him angry. At the same time, when he thought how he had exhausted himself trying to savor the meaning of a lunatic's prose, he felt rather ashamed. Finally, since he had been so deeply impressed by the work of a madman, he could not help wondering whether his own nerves might not be somewhat abnormal too. In this state of mind, anger, shame, and anxiety about his nerves all mingled together, leaving him sitting there with a somewhat distracted expression.

paragraphs.source_en: Just then someone roughly slid open the outer lattice door, and the sound of heavy boots rang twice on the step where shoes are removed. Then the person called out loudly, “Is the master at home? Is the master at home?” The master is not readily moved to get up; Meitei, on the contrary, is a man fond of motion, and without waiting for the maid to go to the entrance and receive the visitor, he called “Come in” and hurried to the doorway in two or three quick strides. It is certainly troublesome that Meitei comes barging into the master's house without so much as asking leave, but once inside he proves useful, for he attends to callers like a houseboy. However informal Meitei may be, he is still a guest, and for this guest to go out to the entrance while Mr. Kushami, the master of the house, sits planted in the parlor without moving is entirely unreasonable. An ordinary man would surely have followed Meitei and shown himself at the doorway, but this is precisely what makes him Mr. Kushami. Unconcerned, he kept his backside settled on the cushion; yet though this composure and ordinary composure may resemble each other in outward flavor, in substance they differ greatly.

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei, who had gone to the entrance, seemed to be talking busily with the visitor for some time, and then shouted loudly toward the inner room, “Hey, master of the house, sorry to trouble you, but please come here a moment. Nothing can be done unless you come.” The master, having no choice, came out slowly with his hands tucked into his sleeves. When he looked, Meitei was holding a visiting card and squatting halfway down as he exchanged words with the visitor. His posture, it seemed, had very little dignity. On the card were printed the words: Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department, Detective Constable Yoshida Torazo. Standing beside this Mr. Torazo was a tall fellow of twenty-five or twenty-six, wearing a dashing outfit entirely of tozan cotton. Strangely enough, this man too, like the master, stood silent with his hands tucked into his sleeves. His face seemed somehow familiar to me, and when I looked more closely, he was not merely someone I had seen before but the very gentleman-burglar who had recently honored us with a midnight visit and carried off the yams. I thought, “Well, well! This time he has deigned to come openly in broad daylight, through the front door.”
